question.problem: In a certain University, professors report that, on average, out of each group of graduate students, $5$ students graduate with the Summa Cum Laude honor. What is the probability that in the next group of graduate students, no more than $3$ students will have the Summa Cum Laude honor? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places. You may assume that receiving the Summa Cum Laude honor occurs independently and at a constant average rate.
question.worked_solution:
A Poisson random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{\lambda }^{x}{e}^{-\lambda }}{x!}
$$

Let $X$ be the number of graduate students with the Summa Cum Laude honor. Since the average rate is $5$ graduates with the Summa Cum Laude honor of each group of graduates, and events occur independently and at a constant average rate, the number of graduate students can be modeled as a Poisson random variable with rate $\lambda =5,$ and we can write $X∼\text{Po}(5).$ 

So, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{5}^{x}{e}^{-5}}{x!}
$$

Therefore, the probability that at most $3$ graduate students will have the Summa Cum Laude honor is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 3) & =P(X\in {0,1,2,3}) \\  & =f(0)+f(1)+f(2)+f(3) \\  & =\frac{{5}^{0}{e}^{-5}}{0!}+\frac{{5}^{1}{e}^{-5}}{1!}+\frac{{5}^{2}{e}^{-5}}{2!}+\frac{{5}^{3}{e}^{-5}}{3!} \\  & ≈0.265\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.
